Yale: handheld uses 'the camera operator's body as a camera support'; 'Newsreel and wartime camera operators favored smaller cameras' later adopted by documentarists; jerky but cheap; 'steadicams were invented in the 1970s and made it possible to create smooth tracking shots.'

Malkiewicz and Mullen: a normal lens reproduces 'perspective similar to that seen by the human eye'; 'in 35mm film, a normal lens is 50mm'; shorter lenses are wide-angle and 'those two or more times longer are telephoto.'

Yale: a wide-angle lens, of short focal length, exaggerates 'the distance between foreground and background planes' and 'allows for more space to enter the frame... convenient for shooting in a closed location, for instance a real room.'

Malkiewicz and Mullen: 'a wide-angle lens exaggerates or elongates depth and a telephoto collapses or compresses it. For example, a person walking toward the camera will seem to approach faster with a wide-angle and slower with a telephoto.'

Malkiewicz and Mullen: perspective 'depends on the camera-to-subject distance and not on the lens'; from the same distance lenses 'change the area of view but do not change the perspective'; 'In a telephoto shot the person is almost always farther away.'

Yale: depth of field is 'The distance through which elements in an image are in sharp focus. Bright light and a narrow lens aperture tend to produce a larger depth of field, as does using a wide-angle rather than a long lens.'

Yale: shallow focus 'keeps only one plane in sharp focus', is 'Used to direct the viewer's attention to one element', and 'is very common in close-up'; a shallow depth of field focuses attention 'without having to use an analytic cut.'

Yale: racking focus changes 'the focus of a lens such that an element in one plane of the image goes out of focus and an element at another plane... comes into focus', steering attention and linking spaces or objects.
Britannica: 'Lighting helps set the tone and emphasize specific parts of a scene.'

Yale: 'Most mainstream films rely on the three-point lighting style'; it is 'The standard lighting scheme for classical narrative cinema': backlight, bright key light, and fill light from the opposite side so the key 'casts only faint shadows.'
Yale: 'Other films, for example documentaries and realist cinema, rely on natural light to create a sense of authenticity.'
Yale: high-key lighting raises the fill 'to almost the same level as the key light', producing bright images with 'few shadows on the principal subjects', characteristic of 'musicals and comedies.'

Yale: low-key lighting 'employs very little fill light, creating strong contrasts' and 'strong shadows that obscure parts of the principal subjects'; associated with suspense genres 'such as film noir.'

Britannica: a slate identifying the take 'topped with a hinged arm'; 'a set of wooden jaws about a foot long, snapped together in the picture field', the clack 'registered on both picture and sound tracks.'
Britannica: the clap gives 'an audible and visual cue' registered on both tracks, enabling alignment of separately recorded sound and picture.

Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film (Editing): 'It is commonly said that a director makes his or her film three times: first, as the screenplay is written; second, as the screenplay is altered at the point of filming; and third, as the material... is changed again in the editing process.'
Schirmer: 'The film editor reviews all of the footage shot on a production, selects the best takes of individual shots, and then orders these'; this 'moves their edit from a rough cut to a fine cut.'
Britannica (film editing): 'The terms editing, cutting, and montage are often...' used for the same process; Yale's glossary lists montage as '1. A synonym for editing.'

Schirmer: 'throughout most of the medium's history, editors worked on celluloid, physically cutting and splicing film using large bulky machines that ran footage in a linear and sequential fashion, from the beginning of a take to its end.'

Science Museum Group: the Moviola, 'a device that allows a film editor to view a film while editing', was the first motion picture editing machine, by Iwan Serrurier in 1924; Schirmer: 'The Moviola was an upright editor with a single screen.'

Schirmer: 'Since the 1990s editors have been working on digital, nonlinear machines, such as Avid', which let an editor 'go instantly to any point in this footage without having to scroll manually through every frame'; the editor 'works at a keyboard.'
Yale: continuity editing is 'A system of cutting to maintain continuous and clear narrative action' that 'relies upon matching screen direction, position, and temporal relations from shot to shot.'

Schirmer: 'The dominant style of editing practiced during the classical Hollywood period, from the 1930s to the 1950s... is sometimes called invisible editing because the edit points are so recessive.'
Yale: 'The film supports the viewer's assumption that space and time are contiguous between successive shots.'

Schirmer describes matching the action on a cut to link shots smoothly; Yale: a 'sense of a consistent space is reinforced by the use of techniques such as the match on action', with shots 'matched on Keaton's actions.'

Schirmer: in the films he made at Biograph from 1908 to 1913, 'matching the action on a cut as a character walks from an exterior into a doorway and, in the next shot, enters an interior set enabled Griffith to join filming locations that were physically separated.'

Yale: the 180 degree rule 'dictates that the camera should stay in one of the areas on either side of the axis of action (an imaginary line drawn between the two major dramatic elements... usually two characters).'

Yale: 'By following this rule the filmmaker ensures that each character occupies a consistent area of the frame'; Schirmer: 'the right-left coordinates of screen geography remain consistent across shot changes.'
Yale: 'The 180 degree line is not usually crossed unless the transition is smoothed by a reestablishing shot.'
Schirmer: editors 'may use continuity cutting to create a stable and reliable spatial geography onscreen, or they may break continuity to undermine spatial coherence.'
Yale: an establishing shot is 'A shot, usually involving a distant framing, that shows the spatial relations among the important figures, objects, and setting in a scene.'
Yale: shot/reverse shot is 'Two or more shots edited together that alternate characters, typically in a conversation situation.'
Schirmer: 'Cut points typically follow the flow of dialogue, and shot-reverse shot editing uses the eyeline match to connect characters who are otherwise shown separately in close-ups.'

Schirmer: 'An editor's decision to play a line of dialogue with the camera on the speaker will inflect the scene in one direction, whereas the decision to use a reaction shot of another character while the line is spoken will give the moment a different tone.'

Schirmer: 'Viewers may attribute to the actor much that' comes from editing, e.g. 'trimming the ends of shots... to make him or her seem to jump on another character's line, or dropping inserts... to draw out the length of an actor's pause.'

Yale: an eyeline match is a cut 'in which the first shot shows a person off in one direction and the second shows a nearby space containing what he or she sees. If the person looks left, the following shot should imply that the looker is offscreen right.'

Yale: crosscutting, aka parallel editing, is 'Editing that alternates shots of two or more lines of action occurring in different places, usually simultaneously. The two actions are therefore linked.'
Schirmer: 'Griffith became famous for his use of crosscutting in the many rides to the rescue that climax his films.'

Schirmer: 'In The Girl and Her Trust (1912)... Griffith cuts back and forth from a pair of robbers, who have abducted the heroine and are escaping on a railroad pump car, to the hero, who is attempting to overtake them by train.'

Schirmer: 'By intercutting these lines of action, Griffith creates suspense, and by shortening the lengths of the shots, he accelerates the pace. Crosscutting furnished a foundation for narrative in cinema.'
Schirmer: editors 'may shrink or contract time by leaving out portions of the action. Jump cuts are an obvious and aestheticized way of doing this'; Breathless's jump cuts 'produce discontinuities.'

Schirmer: 'A bout de souffle (Breathless, 1960), directed by Jean-Luc Godard, used jump cuts that left out parts of the action'; Yale: 'the French Nouvelle Vague films of the 1960s made jump cuts an essential part of their playful, modern outlook.'
Yale: jump cuts 'suggest the ruminations or ambivalences of a character' and are 'a clear signifier of rupture with mainstream film storytelling', showing 'the artificiality' of the telling.

Yale: a graphic match is 'Two successive shots joined so as to create a strong similarity of compositional elements (e.g., color, shape)', used 'to smooth the transition' or 'to make metaphorical associations.'

LoC National Film Registry essay: 'When the man-ape then tosses his newfound weapon/tool end-over-end and the tumbling bone turns into an orbiting satellite, Kubrick makes the cinema's most famous jump-cut and eye rhyme'; NASA calls it a 'match cut.'
Britannica: Kuleshov (1899-1970) was 'a Soviet film theorist and director who taught that structuring a film by montage... was the most important aspect of filmmaking.'
Britannica: an actor's neutral expression followed by soup, a child, or a corpse; 'audiences interpreted the actor's emotion as hunger, tenderness, or grief, respectively.'
Britannica: 'the shot in film always has two values: the one it carries in itself as a photographic image of reality and the one it acquires when placed into juxtaposition with another shot.'
PLOS ONE (2024): 'In the glance shot, a character is shown gazing toward an offscreen entity (in this instance, Mozhukin's neutral face), whereas the object shot captures the item being looked at.'

Barratt et al. (Lund): 'The original film footage is lost'; Schirmer says Kuleshov 'allegedly' used soup, a grieving woman at a gravestone and a child, a different list from Britannica's soup, child and corpse.

Schirmer: 'it is extremely doubtful that Kuleshov's experiment worked exactly as he claimed (for one thing, it is likely that the actor's face actually contained an ambiguous expression since Kuleshov had taken the footage from an existing film).'

Barratt et al. (2016): 'recent attempts at replication have produced either conflicting or unreliable results'; with '36 participants', 'The results suggest that some sort of Kuleshov effect does in fact exist.'
Yale: 'The diegesis includes objects, events, spaces and the characters that inhabit them, including things, actions, and attitudes not explicitly presented in the film but inferred by the audience.'
Yale: 'Any voice, musical passage, or sound effect presented as originating from a source within the film's world is diegetic.'
Yale: 'If it originates outside the film (as most background music) then it is non-diegetic'; the score is 'a common example of non-diegetic sound, sounds that only the spectators can hear.'
Yale: sounds that 'exist only in Anna's troubled mind... are internal diegetic sounds (inside of a character's mind) that no one else in the gallery can hear.'
Britannica: a Foley artist creates sounds synchronized with specific on-screen actions, such as footsteps, a sword fight or a creaking door.
Britannica: 'In the first few decades of talkies, microphones were designed mainly to pick up spoken dialogue', so other sounds had to be added.

Britannica: 'Jack Foley, who almost single-handedly developed the craft as motion pictures made the transition to sound'; at Universal on Show Boat, 'Foley and his crew simultaneously added clapping, laughter, and other sounds' as the film ran 'in real time.'
Britannica: Foley artists work in studios with props such as shoes and a large screen to view the scene, performing sounds in sync.
Britannica: Foley artists used frozen lettuce for the frost sounds in Titanic.

SoundGirls: 'The term sound designer was used for the first time in film in 1979. Francis Ford Coppola granted Walter Murch the title of Sound Designer for his work on Apocalypse Now, marking the first use of the term as a credit in film'; NFTS: Murch 'introduced the credit.'
SoundGirls: 'Murch oversaw the overall sound concept of the film, including dialogue, sound effects, foley, and the final mix.'
Yale: a sound bridge occurs 'when the sound from the previous scene carries over briefly' or 'when the sound from the next scene is heard before the image appears on the screen.'
Yale: 'Sound bridges are one of the most common transitions in the continuity editing style, one that stresses the connection between both scenes.'

Britannica (sound era): 'Warner Brothers, then a minor studio in the midst of aggressive expansion, bought both the system and the right to sublease it', debuting it with Don Juan (1926); Britannica's Jazz Singer entry names the Vitaphone sound-on-disc system.
Britannica: 'the first feature-length movie with synchronized dialogue'; only 'the musical numbers and some select conversations amounting to one-fourth of the film were recorded for sound.'
Britannica: The Jazz Singer's 'phenomenal success virtually ensured the industry's conversion to sound.'
Britannica: Al Jolson stars as Jakie Rabinowitz; 'His blackface performance remains studied for its implications regarding stereotypes and ethnic assimilation.'
PBS American Experience (Dale Cockrell): 'It need hardly be said that minstrelsy is about racial derision'; Mel Watkins traces stereotypes such as Uncle Tom to minstrelsy.

Britannica: 'The wholesale conversion to sound of all three sectors of the American film industry took place in less than 15 months between late 1927 and 1929', with studios and theaters completely reequipped.
Britannica: early microphones 'had a very limited range', so actors were 'forced to remain practically motionless' while speaking toward them.

Britannica: 'cameras and their operators were initially enclosed in soundproof glass-paneled booths... facetiously called iceboxes because they were uncomfortably hot', which kept the camera from moving.
Britannica: 'by 1931 all the studios had removed their cameras from the iceboxes and converted to the use of lightweight soundproof camera housings known as blimps.'

problem: Emil Jannings did not stop finding work in sound films. His accent ended his Hollywood career, but he returned to Germany and starred in sound films there, most famously The Blue Angel (1930). The cited Science and Its Times entry overstates it.
proposed: The switch to sound ended some silent careers in Hollywood: the German star Emil Jannings, whose heavy accent suited no English-speaking role, left Hollywood and went back to making films in Germany, including the sound film The Blue Angel (1930). (Card 041.c4: change 'Some great silent stars could no longer find work in sound films, among them the German actor Emil Jannings, whose heavy accent had never been heard on a silent screen.' to 'Some silent stars' careers did not survive the switch: the German actor Emil Jannings, whose heavy accent had never been heard on a silent screen, had to leave Hollywood and went back to making films in Germany.')
evidence: Britannica: 'With the advent of sound in American cinema, Jannings was forced because of his thick accent to abandon his career in the United States. He continued to work in German films'; he starred in Der blaue Engel (1930).
Britannica: by 1930 '95 percent of all American production was concentrated in the hands of only eight studios.'

Britannica: the five majors (MGM, Paramount, Warner Brothers, Fox and RKO) controlled production, distribution and exhibition; Universal, Columbia and United Artists did not own major theater chains (Encyclopedia.com's 1950s history: the three minors 'did not own' theaters).
Britannica: after acquiring first-run theater chains in the 1920s the majors functioned as 'diversified theater chains, producing features, shorts, cartoons, and newsreels to fill their houses.'

US v. Paramount (1948): 'Block-booking is the practice of licensing, or offering for license, one feature or group of features on condition that the exhibitor will also license another feature or group of features released by the distributors during a given period.'
National Women's History Museum: 'because actors were typically required to remain anonymous, Lawrence became famous as the Biograph girl.'
NWHM: in 1910 Lawrence was hired by Carl Laemmle 'for his new studio called the Independent Motion Picture Company (IMP)', which publicized her; she was 'one of the first motion picture stars.'
Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film (Publicity and Promotion): 'The film star was perhaps the most important development in film advertising.'

Schirmer: studios controlled stars' images 'through a variety of means including morality clauses in contracts and careful publicity'; publicists 'provided copy and photos for the fan magazines, including intimate confessions.'
Schirmer refers to 'the court decision that the standard seven-year' star contract could not be extended; Britannica's de Havilland entry also describes her seven-year contract.

Britannica: 'In 1945 de Havilland won a precedent-setting case against Warner Brothers, which released her from a six-month penalty obligation appended by the studio to her seven-year contract'; she then won Oscars for To Each His Own (1946) and The Heiress (1949).
Britannica: studio leaders formed the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America in 1922 and recruited Will H. Hays to lead it.
Britannica: Martin Quigley and Daniel A. Lord drafted more stringent guidelines, which the MPPDA adopted in 1930.
Britannica: 'a set of self-imposed guidelines by Hollywood studios that regulated the moral content of films', arising from 'public outcry and the threat of government censorship.'

Britannica: Catholic prelates 'formed the Legion of Decency, which created its own film-rating system and called for boycotts'; in 1934 the Production Code Administration was set up under Joseph Breen.
Britannica: 'Members of the MPPDA... agreed to distribute only films that were PCA-approved.'
Britannica: the code prohibited 'profanity, obscenity, and graphic depictions of violence, criminality'; Hays Code entry: 'evil and good are never confused.'
Britannica: 'the proliferation of television shows and the increasing availability of foreign films, both of which fell outside the PCA's jurisdiction', undermined the code after World War II.
Britannica: the 1952 Supreme Court ruling in Burstyn v. Wilson held that films are protected by the First Amendment, undermining the case for censorship.
Britannica: the code regulated films from 1934 to 1968, when 'the industry replaced this standards system with the modern motion-picture rating system that remains in use today.'
Britannica: the three-strip process, 'perfected in 1932', used 'a beam-splitting optical cube' to expose three black-and-white films, each recording one of red, green or blue.
Britannica: the three strips were developed separately, dyed and laminated together, producing 'a reasonably faithful approximation of natural colour.'

Britannica: a practical commercial colour system arrived when Technicolor debuted in Disney's Flowers and Trees (1932) and the feature Becky Sharp (1935); FIAF Film Atlas agrees (first three-color cartoon; first three-color live-action feature).
George Eastman Museum: 'Technicolor's three-color camera weighed 200 pounds and cost in excess of $10,000 to manufacture.'
FIAF Film Atlas: Technicolor 'retained exclusive rights and rented them to studios'; it 'provided color consultants (headed by Natalie Kalmus) to each production.'

FIAF Film Atlas: 'In the early 1950s, the company started a transition to making imbibition prints from Eastmancolor negatives'; Foxfire and The Ladykillers (1955) 'were among the last productions photographed using Technicolor cameras.'

Britannica: 'The introduction of colour was less revolutionary than the introduction of sound; the silent film soon disappeared, but, even though most feature films made since the 1960s have been in colour, black-and-white films continue to be made.'
Britannica: released in 1941 by RKO; Welles directed, produced, co-wrote with Herman J. Mankiewicz and starred, at 25.
LoC National Film Registry essay: released by RKO in 1941 'to considerable critical acclaim but disappointing box-office returns; at the Oscars it won only best screenplay.'

Britannica: Toland used new faster Eastman stock, wide-angle lenses and high-intensity arc lamps to achieve 'a photographic depth of field that approximated the perceptual range of the human eye'; Encyclopedia.com's Toland entry adds coated lenses and arc lamps.
Encyclopedia.com (Toland): 'For the first time, audiences could see sharply detailed characters and objects in all parts of the screen in nearly every scene.'

Encyclopedia.com: 'Instead of lighting from rafters on sets that had no ceilings, as had been the custom up until then, Toland had muslin ceilings constructed, enabling sound mikes to be placed above them.'
LoC NFR essay: 'In the 1940s, Welles's dramatic chiaroscuro, low-angled shots that revealed ceilings, crystalline depth-of-field, and so on, appeared powerful, modern, hyperarticulate.'

LoC NFR essay: Kane 'recounts Kane's life via the shifting, not always reliable testimonies of five former intimates, a technique Welles called prismatic'; Britannica: it opens with Kane's death and a reporter's investigation.
Britannica: Citizen Kane remains 'one of the most influential films ever made.'

Britannica: from 1947 HUAC investigated communist influence in Hollywood; 'More than 100 witnesses... were called before the committee to answer questions about their own and their associates' alleged communist affiliations.' Britannica's HUAC entry: established 1938.

Britannica: HUAC held that 'the Communist movement in the United States is foreign-controlled' and 'an immediate and powerful threat to the security of the United States'; UW-Madison WCFTR: the committee's concern was communist propaganda 'infiltrating Hollywood films.'
WCFTR: 'The Ten invoked the First Amendment in refusing to answer government inquiries into their private beliefs and political associations'; Britannica: eight screenwriters and two directors.
Britannica: the Ten were convicted of contempt of Congress and sentenced to six months to one year in prison.

Britannica: studio heads 'published what became known as the Waldorf Declaration, in which they fired the members of the Hollywood Ten'; studios then refused to employ anyone 'even suspected of having communist associations.'
Britannica: most of the Ten never again worked in Hollywood; some wrote under assumed names, and Trumbo won an Academy Award as Robert Rich for The Brave One (1956).
Britannica: in 1960 Trumbo 'received full credit for the motion-picture epics Exodus and Spartacus'; Britannica's Hollywood Ten entry: the blacklist had faded by the early 1960s.
Britannica: HUAC was criticized for 'violating First Amendment rights', declined in influence by the 1960s, was renamed in 1969 and dissolved in 1975.
LII text of 334 U.S. 131: 'Decided May 3, 1948'; 'Mr. Justice DOUGLAS delivered the opinion of the Court'; the defendants were held to have violated the Sherman Act.

334 U.S. 131: the District Court found defendants 'fixed minimum admission prices which the exhibitors agreed to charge' and held block-booking illegal; the Court found 'adequate foundation' for the price-fixing conspiracies and approved the block-booking ruling.
334 U.S. 131: 'In the 92 cities of the country with populations over 100,000 at least 70 per cent of all the first-run theatres are affiliated with one or more of the five majors.'
Britannica: the 'Paramount decrees... forced the studios to divest themselves of their theater chains and mandated competition in the exhibition sector for the first time in 30 years.'
History of the American Cinema (Encyclopedia.com): 'By cutting the link between production and exhibition, the consent decrees made film production a much less stable undertaking.'
Britannica: 'The industry was more severely weakened in 1948, when a federal antitrust suit against the five major and three minor studios ended in the Paramount decrees.'
Britannica: record profits in 1946, when 'two-thirds of the American population went to the movies at least once a week.'
Britannica: 'the advent of network television broadcasting in the 1940s provided Hollywood with its first real competition for American leisure time by offering consumers movies in the home.'
History of the American Cinema: 'by 1956 attendance was down almost 50 percent from the 1946 peak.'
History of the American Cinema: 'Hollywood put greater emphasis on A productions, and eventually on color and widescreen, to differentiate itself from television.'
Britannica: 'three synchronized movie projectors each project[ing] one-third of the picture on a wide, curving screen'; This Is Cinerama was 'presented in New York City in 1952.'
Britannica: a popular novelty whose 'prohibitive' costs led to its abandonment in the 1960s.
Britannica: a special camera lens squeezed a wide image onto standard 35 mm film and a projection lens restored it, with 'the width of the image two and a half times its height.'
Britannica: Twentieth Century-Fox debuted CinemaScope with The Robe (1953); by the late 1950s wide-screen had become standard at the major studios.
Britannica: between 1930 and 1945 every stage of production, 'from conception through exhibition, was carefully controlled.'
